intent: Function: the head walks right past each mark and marks the next blank, so three marks become four.
content: The head steps along three marks and turns the first empty cell into a fourth because two rules decide every step (on a mark, move right; on an empty cell, write and stop), so 3 + 1 = 4 is computed by rule-following alone.
knows: Tally marks; following written instructions one at a time.
subtraction: Reread ch1-context-p4 and p5: the tape, the head, rules for each symbol and state, and the universal machine, all in the abstract. Lost: the device seen working, two rules adding one (3 + 1 = 4) step by step. Keep.

intent: Real thing: the rotors step before each press, so the same key lights a different lamp every time.
content: The rotors step before each press, so the current runs key, three rotors, reflector and back by a new path: A lights F, then E, then C. The reflector sends it back by another path, so no letter ever lights itself (ch1-context-p9), the flaw the codebreakers used.
knows: A typewriter keyboard; a battery lighting a bulb through a wire.
subtraction: Reread ch1-context-p8 (cites it): Enigma's 158 quintillion settings, its never-itself flaw and the Bombe, but not how the machine works. Lost: what the machine is (keyboard, rotors, reflector, lamps) and one key lighting a different lamp at each press. Keep.

intent: Real thing: a glowing tube and a sliver of crystal each let a small signal switch a large current.
content: A glowing vacuum tube and a sliver of crystal each let a small control signal switch a large current because both are the same switch, so the transistor does the tube's job with no glass, filament or heat to burn out.
knows: A light switch; vacuum tubes as glass bulbs controlling current (ch1-transistor-p1).
subtraction: Reread ch1-transistor-p1, p2, p4 and p5: p1 describes the tube as a glass bulb with a heated filament (ENIAC's 17,468); p2 gives the transistor's invention as the tube's replacement; p4 the transistor as a switch worked by its base; p5 off and on as 0 and 1, and AND. Nothing describes the transistor's look or sets the two side by side. Lost: a tube and a transistor side by side as they look, each switched by one small signal; 'the same job' is said only in the caption (ch1-transistor-p3). Half of one idea with Fig 1.4. Merge: the merged card is Fig 1.4 at its slot, after ch1-transistor-p4 and p5; fig-1-3 and its caption ch1-transistor-p3 alias to ch1-transistor-p2.
concepts_tried: Concepts for the merged card (drafted 2026-10-24 while the calibration page is up; stills only). B: one lamp circuit, the switch slot holding a tube on one side and a transistor on the other (its still shows only 'on'; the off state needs motion). C: the two at true relative scale on a 10 cm ruler (scale, but no function).
chosen: See Fig 1.4's row: the merged card's concept lives there.

content: Top: a glowing vacuum tube (1906) and a transistor (1947) drawn as they look, one small control signal switching each, both lamps lit. Below: the lamp stays dark at 0 V on the base and lights at 0.7 V because the base voltage opens the path from collector to emitter, so one small voltage turns a current off or on: 0 or 1.
knows: A light switch; a battery lighting a lamp through a wire; vacuum tubes as glass bulbs controlling current (ch1-transistor-p1).
subtraction: Reread ch1-transistor-p4 and p5: base, collector and emitter and the switch, in words; p5 adds AND. A Function card; the top panel is checked, not scored.

intent: Function: a positive gate pulls electrons under the oxide into a channel, so current flows only while it is on.
content: Electrons gather under the oxide into a channel when the gate goes positive because the gate's field pulls them up from the n-type source and drain (silicon with spare electrons) into the p-type body between, without touching them, so current flows only while the gate is on.
knows: A rubbed balloon lifting hair; a transistor as a switch (ch1-transistor-p4).
subtraction: Reread ch1-transistor-p7 and p18 (p18 cites it): doping, source, drain and gate, the barrier and the bridge of electrons, in dense words. Lost: the channel seen forming under the gate at 1 V and absent at 0 V. Keep.

chosen: B: the same cross-section at 0 V and at 1 V, the lower one switching on each cycle; the still alone shows the switch. Draft f7bfec6, Gate 1 clean; not yet judged.

intent: Function: transistor counts doubled about every two years, so on a tenfold-per-step scale they rise in a straight line.
content: The count of transistors per chip climbs a straight line on a log scale because it doubled about every two years, so 2,300 in 1971 becomes 28 billion in 2024, and the M4 falls below the line.
knows: Doubling (1, 2, 4, 8); a chart with years along the bottom.
subtraction: Reread ch1-transistor-p10 (Moore's doubling, its revision to two years, its end around 2015, as a claim) and p15 and p16 (2,300 transistors in the 4004, 28 billion in the M4, the slowdown since about 2015). Lost: the chips in between (8086 to Epyc) lying on a straight line on a log scale, and the last dot (the M4) dropping below it. Phase 2: the axis label's 'log scale' is first explained in the caption, so the redraw labels the gridlines ('each line ten times the last') instead. Keep.

intent: Real thing: a room of tubes and a fingertip chip do the same switching; the switch shrank to a speck.
content: ENIAC's thirty metres of cabinets and the M4 under a fingertip stand side by side, each at its own scale, because both do the same job of switching, so 17,468 tubes against 28 billion transistors shows 79 years of shrinking.
knows: A room full of cabinets; a fingertip; Fig 1.6's doubling.
subtraction: Reread ch1-transistor-p1 (thirty metres of cabinets, 17,468 tubes) and p16 (the M4's 28 billion transistors). Lost: the two seen side by side, a room of cabinets against a fingertip chip, each at its own scale; the 1.6 million ratio is only in its caption. Keep.

intent: Function: the program sits in memory beside its data, so the CPU fetches each instruction like a number.
content: Instructions and numbers travel one at a time from one memory over one bus to the CPU because the program is stored as numbers beside its data, so as the program counter steps through cells 0, 1 and 2, load A, add B, store C turns 5 and 3 into 8 in cell C.
knows: Numbered boxes holding notes; Fig 1.1's head following stored rules.
subtraction: Reread ch1-vonneumann-p3 and p4 (p4 walks the figure cell by cell and cites it; ch1-cpu-p2 and ch2-arithmetic-p7 cite it too). Lost: one memory holding program and data, seen, as load A, add B and store C run over the bus. The prose depends on it. Keep.

intent: Function: the program counter advances by each instruction's length until an instruction sets it back, so the program loops.
content: The program counter moves 0x00, 0x05, 0x08 and back to 0x00 because each writeback advances it by the instruction's length and the jump at 0x08 sets it back, so the program runs the same three instructions again and again; the four-step cycle itself repeats for every instruction.
knows: Fig 1.8's memory cells; a recipe followed step by step.
subtraction: Reread ch1-cpu-p1 and p2 (p2 cites it): the four steps and instructions of different lengths, in words. Lost: the program counter seen stepping by each instruction's length (0x00, 0x05, 0x08) and jumping back. Keep.

intent: Function: the assembler turns mov eax, 5 into bytes: first the operation and register, then the value.
content: mov eax, 5 becomes five bytes, B8 05 00 00 00, because the assembler writes one byte for the operation and register and four for the value, lowest byte first, so the CPU reads B8 as "into EAX" and the rest as 5.
knows: Fig 1.9's instructions in memory; writing a number in digits.
subtraction: Reread ch1-cpu-p4 and p5: the ISA, assembly, and the bits of mov eax, 5 written out. Lost: the byte roles (one byte for the operation and register, four for the value), which Fig 3.1 also carries (its row), and byte order: 'lowest byte first' appears only in this card and its caption (ch1-cpu-p6). No later passage depends on the order of a value's bytes in memory (Fig 3.1's x86 value is one byte, Fig 3.3 reads a register, Fig 9.4 reads fields whole); p5's bit string keeps its stored order unexplained, accepted under law 4. A cut drops the parenthetical '(Fig 1.10 takes one apart)' from Fig 1.9's How it works.

intent: Function: stages overlap like an assembly line, so once the line is full one instruction finishes every cycle.
content: Five instructions overlap stage by stage because each stage takes the next instruction as soon as it is free, so they finish in 9 cycles instead of 25, one instruction per cycle once the line is full.
knows: An assembly line or a laundry queue; Fig 1.9's four steps.

intent: Function: jobs ran one at a time, and the machine sat idle while the operator loaded each next deck.
content: One job ran at a time; between jobs the machine sat idle while the operator loaded the next card deck (about 25 idle minutes in an illustrative hour; your job runs ten). Drawn on a 9:00 to 10:00 timeline: a 'you · waiting' lane and a CPU lane, your job ('yours') among the others, 'running a job' against 'idle: the next deck loading'. ch1-kernel-p3's idleness during a job, waiting for I/O, is a separate point.

Lost: the idle gaps between jobs while the operator loads the next deck, about 25 minutes of the illustrative hour; p1 does not mention them. Keep.

intent: Function: a program cannot reach the disk itself; it must ask the kernel, which checks and does the work.
content: A program's direct reach for the disk is blocked while its system call goes through a fixed entry because the CPU runs programs in Ring 3 and the kernel in Ring 0, so the kernel checks every request and drives the device itself.
knows: A bank clerk fetches from the vault for you; time-sharing, programs taking turns (ch1-kernel-p4).
subtraction: Reread ch1-kernel-p4 (cites it: time-sharing, the kernel, asking the kernel) and p6 after it (the program cannot touch the disk, asks through a system call, the kernel checks and does the work; Ring 3 and Ring 0). Lost: the privilege boundary seen as nested layers, the CPU stopping the direct reach; the blocked-against-asked mechanism is in p6's words, after the card. Ring 0, Ring 3 and 'system call' are first named in its caption (ch1-kernel-p5), so the redraw labels by role (programs, kernel, asks the kernel) and puts the names in the strip. Keep.

The picture the name comes from. intent: Function: each level down is bigger but slower, so a cache keeps recent reads close and repeats are fast.
content: Each level from registers down to disk is bigger and slower (one second to six months, at a human scale) because faster memory costs more per byte, so a cache keeps what was just read and the second read takes 4 s instead of 3 min.
knows: A desk, a shelf and a library across town.
subtraction: Reread ch1-memory-p1 and p2: the hierarchy and three raw times (0.3 ns, 60 ns, 50,000 ns). Lost: the levels side by side at a human time scale, a register in a second, a disk in months. Keep.

intent: Function: binary splits a wire's voltage into two wide bands, so noise that tips ternary's narrow bands leaves binary right.
content: The same noise jostles two wires with the same span because binary splits it into two bands and ternary into three narrower ones, so binary reads all five bits right while ternary misreads its fourth digit.
knows: An on/off switch against a dimmer; a transistor switched by a voltage (ch1-transistor-p4).
subtraction: Reread ch2-binary-p2 and p3: one threshold against two, and narrow bands misread under drift, in words. Lost: the same noise on two wires, binary reading all five bits right and ternary misreading its fourth digit. Keep.

intent: Function: Boole's AND and two switches in series agree in every case, so algebra and circuit are one rule.
content: Boole's A · B and Shannon's two switches in series give the same answer in every case because each is true only when both inputs are, so the algebra of 1847 and the circuit of 1937 are one AND.
knows: And in everyday speech; two switches in a row (ch1-transistor-p5).
subtraction: Reread ch2-boole-p3 (AND true only when both are) and p6 (two relays in series as AND). Lost: the two halves side by side, Boole's overlap of two circles and two switches in series, as one rule. Already two panels. Keep.

intent: Function: as inputs step through every case, each gate's output follows its table: AND both, OR either, NOT the opposite.
content: Each standard symbol (AND, OR, NOT) beside its truth table, the inputs stepping through every case and each output following its rule. The section's three HTML truth tables sit above the card; the switches inside each gate (two in series for AND, two in parallel for OR, two taking turns for NOT) are told in ch2-gates-p2.

subtraction: Reread ch2-gates-p1 and p2, and the section's three HTML truth tables above p2 (AND, OR and NOT, each under its rule heading). Lost: the standard symbols (the flat back, the curved back, the bubble), which Figs 2.4 to 2.6 draw on, and the inputs stepping through every case beside them; the tables themselves are in the prose. intent: Function: NAND is AND inverted, so tied inputs give NOT and inverting again gives AND: one gate builds all.
content: NOT, AND and OR are wired from NAND gates alone and give the same truth tables because NAND is AND inverted and two inversions cancel, so one kind of gate can build any circuit.
knows: Fig 2.3's three gates and their tables.
subtraction: Reread ch2-gates-p4 and p5: all three NAND constructions walked in words; no prose cites the figure (p4 points only at the De Morgan box). Lost: the three wirings seen at once as the inputs step through every case; p4 asks the reader to hold all three in mind. Keep.

intent: Function: each column needs the carry from its right, so carries ripple left and the answer settles bit by bit.
content: Adding 0101 and 0011, each full adder waits for the carry from its right-hand neighbour because a column's sum depends on it, so the carry ripples left and 1000 (8) settles one bit at a time.
knows: Carrying in column addition by hand; Fig 2.3's gates.
subtraction: Reread ch2-arithmetic-p5 to p7: the full adder and the ripple-carry chain, in words (cited by ch2-arithmetic-p9). Lost: the carry seen rippling left as 5 + 3 settles into 1000, one bit at a time. Keep.

intent: Function: the second half adder adds the carry-in to the first sum; an OR merges their carries, never both 1.
content: Inside one full adder, two half adders (XOR for the sum, AND for the carry) and an OR produce sum and carry-out because XOR is 1 when the bits differ and AND when both are 1, so all eight input cases come out right.
knows: Fig 2.5's full adder as a box; Fig 2.3's gates.
subtraction: Reread ch2-arithmetic-p3 to p5: p5 gives the full adder in words (two half adders, the second adds the carry-in, the OR merges their carries, never both 1). Lost: the wiring seen, and the eight cases that let the reader check p5's claim that the two carries are never both 1. Keep.

intent: Function: adding a number's two's-complement pattern and dropping the carry out subtracts it, so the adder does both.
content: 7 plus 11111011 (the 8-bit pattern for −5: 5's bits flipped, plus 1) runs on the ordinary adder and a ninth bit falls off because 11111011 is 256 − 5 and the register holds eight bits, so exactly 2 remains: subtraction done by addition.
knows: Column addition (Fig 2.5); a car's odometer rolling over.
subtraction: Reread ch2-twos-p5 and p6: p6 works 7 − 5 in full (7 + 251 = 256 + 2, the ninth place dropped) and gives the hardware (NOT gates, a carry-in of 1). Lost: the bits seen in columns with the ninth bit falling off. Half of one idea with Fig 2.8: both are the byte's wrap. Merge: the merged card is Fig 2.8 at its slot, after ch2-twos-p8; fig-2-7 and its caption ch2-twos-p7 alias to ch2-twos-p6.

intent: Function: a byte's values wrap round a wheel, so dropping the carry subtracts, and adding past the top turns negative.
content: Top: 7 plus 11111011 (−5: 5's bits flipped, plus 1) on the ordinary adder, the ninth bit falling off and 2 left. Below: a wheel of 256 values, the half whose top bit is 1 read as negatives; a pointer turns one notch per +1, so −1 + 1 lands on 0 (the carry dropped, correct) and +127 + 1 on −128 (overflow, a silent wrap).
knows: A clock face wrapping past 12; a car's odometer rolling over; column addition (Fig 2.5).
subtraction: Reread ch2-twos-p8 (the ranges only) and p10 (cites the bottom of the wheel; it leads into held Fig 2.9). Lost: the wrap seen, +127 + 1 becoming −128 and −1 + 1 becoming 0. Keep, as the merged card with Fig 2.7. Its three citations (ch2-twos-p10, ch5-ub-p3, held Fig 2.9's card) stay valid, since the merged card keeps the number 2.8.

intent: Function: a sign, an exponent that moves the point and the digits rebuild 6.5 straight from a double's bits.
content: 6.5 and −0.75 are read straight off their bits because a double stores a sign, an exponent that moves the point and a mantissa of digits, so 1.625 × 2² = 6.5 appears from the three fields. The labels use the exponent bias (stored 1025 − 1023 = 2, 1022 − 1023 = −1), which ch2-float-p6 teaches only after the card: Phase 2 explains it in the figure or moves p6's sentence ahead of the card.

intent: Function: stored 0.1 and 0.2 run slightly high, so their sum lands halfway between doubles and the tie rounds up.
content: On a line drawn to scale near 0.3, the true sum of the stored 0.1 and 0.2 falls exactly halfway between two doubles because both stored values sit slightly high, so the tie rounds up and prints 0.30000000000000004. A first panel shows 0.1 in binary (0.0 0011 0011 ... repeating forever), which ch2-float-p2 already gives in words. The strip's result line says the rounded values 'add up to the one just above'; the sum lands on the tie first (p7): Phase 2 fixes the strip.
knows: Rounding to the nearest; 1/3 never ending in decimal.
subtraction: Reread ch2-float-p6 and p7: the stored values running high, the tie and its rule, in words. Lost: the tie seen to scale (the stored 0.3, the true sum halfway, the double it rounds to). Keep.

intent: Function: each tick of a tenth of a second ran slightly short, so the error grew until the radar missed.
content: The clock's error grows tick by tick to 0.34 s after 100 hours because 0.1 was stored cut short, a little under a ten-millionth of a second per tick, and each tick added the shortfall, so the radar looked about 570 m from the Scud and the battery never fired.
knows: Fig 2.11's 0.1 that binary cannot hold exactly; a clock running slow.
subtraction: Reread ch2-float-p11: fixed point chopping 0.1, and the shortfall growing over 100 hours, in words. Lost: the drift seen growing, and its size (0.34 s, about 570 m), which only the figure and its caption give; p11 has neither number. Keep.

intent: Function: each instruction set encodes the same add in its own bits, so a program for one fails on another.
content: Add 5 to a register as 32 bits in three instruction sets: x86-64 add rax, 5 (48 83 C0 05, with a 64-bit prefix, the opcode, rax and the 5), ARM64 add x0, x0, 5 (0x91001400) and RISC-V addi a0, a0, 5 (0x00550513), each with its opcode, register name and the 5 in different places and other fields grey, so a program built for one instruction set means nothing to another.
knows: An instruction as bytes in memory (Fig 1.9).
subtraction: Reread ch3-isa-p1 and p2: the ISA as a contract and the three ISAs; p4 after it says the encodings differ. Lost: the same add packed three ways (opcode, register, the number 5 in three orders), which is why a binary fails on another ISA. It also carries the byte roles Fig 1.10 shows. Keep.

intent: Function: ARM cannot add in memory, so Rosetta 2 rewrites each Intel add in memory as load, add and store.
content: Three Intel lines and the Rosetta 2 box become six ARM lines, each with a plain note (put 5 in register w8, store w8 in memory, load it into w8, add 3, store it, load it into w0); a key marks [ ] as memory. ARM cannot add in memory, so it must load, add and store; Rosetta 2 translates the app once, before it runs. The caption (ch3-isa-p5) accounts for five of the six lines; Phase 2 fixes it.
knows: Fig 3.1's different encodings; translating a sentence phrase by phrase.
subtraction: Reread ch3-isa-p4 (Rosetta 2 in words), p6 (RISC computes only in registers and reaches memory through loads and stores, 'which is why Fig 3.2's three x86 lines became six') and ch3-registers-p1 (load, add, store). Lost: the concrete translation, the three Intel lines and the six ARM lines with their notes. Keep.

intent: Function: each widening kept the older, smaller names inside the new one, so EAX is the lower half of RAX.
content: One 64-bit register is shown nested as RAX, EAX, AX, then AH and AL because each generation (1978, 1985, 2003) widened it and kept the old names, so writing AL changes one byte and writing EAX clears the upper half.
knows: Registers as the fastest memory (Fig 1.15); mov eax, 5 (ch1-cpu-p5).
subtraction: Reread ch3-registers-p1 and p2: 16 registers of 64 bits and six roles (RAX, RDI, RSI, RSP, RBP, RIP). Lost: the nesting seen, RAX holding EAX holding AX split into AH and AL, with dates; AX, AH and AL appear only in the card and its caption. Keep.

intent: Function: a shared convention fixes where arguments and the result go, so compilers following it can call each other's code.
content: work(a, b, c, d, e, f, g) puts 1 to 6 in RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8 and R9 in order and the seventh on the stack, and the result comes back in RAX into r, under the System V convention that compilers on Linux and macOS share; Windows uses other registers and needs a wrapper (ch3-call-p2). The prose's worked example is add(5, 3) in EDI and ESI (ch3-call-p3).
knows: Fig 3.3's registers; handing things over in an agreed order.
subtraction: Reread ch3-registers-p2 and its summary table (RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8 and R9 as the first six argument registers, RAX for the result) and ch3-call-p2 and p3 (the System V convention, Windows' other registers, and add(5, 3) in EDI and ESI). intent: Function: the stack starts high and grows down: each call extends it and each return shrinks it.
content: A process's memory runs from code and data at the bottom, the heap growing up and the stack growing down from under the kernel because the operating system gives every process the same layout, so each call adds a frame and each return removes it.
knows: Fig 1.8's numbered memory; a stack of plates.
subtraction: Reread ch3-stack-p1 to p4: the address space and the stack placed high and growing down (p1), push and pop (p3), and frames created at each call and discarded at each return, with the heap named once (p4, citing the card). The heap and the layout must survive Phase 2: ch3-stack-p4 cites the card for the heap, and Figs 5.6, BR.4 and 16.1 lean on the layout. Keep.

intent: Function: call pushes the return address onto the stack and jumps; ret pops it into RIP, so the caller resumes.
content: The stack and RIP change step by step through one call of add because call saves where to come back to and ret jumps there, so the program carries on exactly after the call with the result in RAX.
knows: Fig 3.5's stack growing down; Fig 1.9's program counter.

intent: Function: the CPU checks a privilege bit, so in Ring 3 a privileged instruction never runs; the kernel takes over.
content: The same three instructions run in Ring 3 and in Ring 0 because the CPU checks a privilege bit on each, so add runs in both while the two privileged ones stop at #GP in Ring 3 and jump to the kernel's handler.
knows: Fig 1.14's rings.
subtraction: Reread chBridge-mode-p3 and p4: the CPU checking the CPL, #GP, and the Ring 0 instructions, in words. Lost: the same three instructions in each ring side by side, add running in both and the two privileged ones stopping at #GP in Ring 3. Keep.

intent: Function: SYSCALL jumps to an address the kernel chose, so a program picks the service, never the destination.
content: One write call crosses from Ring 3 to Ring 0 and back because SYSCALL saves where to return and jumps to an address the kernel registered, with the request number in RAX, so the program picks the service but never the destination, and SYSRET brings it back in under a microsecond.
knows: Fig BR.1's privilege bit; Fig 1.14's system call.
subtraction: Reread chBridge-trap-p1 and p2 (p2 cites it, as does chBridge-trap-p4): the trap, the number in RAX, SYSCALL, the saved address and SYSRET, in words. Lost: the round trip in time order, with the registers that carry it. Keep.

intent: Function: a vector number picks an entry in the kernel's table, and the CPU jumps to that entry's handler.
content: A vector number picks one of 256 entries and the CPU jumps to that entry's handler because the kernel filled the table at boot and IDTR points to it, so exceptions (0–31), device interrupts (32 and up) and int 0x80 all enter the kernel the same way. Its caption (chBridge-trap-p5) has three sentences: with the owner's yes the Phase 2 rebuild cuts it to two; without it the caption stays and READY lists it.
knows: Fig BR.2's trap; a building directory pointing to rooms.

intent: Function: the MMU translates every address and checks its permissions, so a forbidden access never reaches memory.
content: A virtual address passes through the MMU before it reaches RAM because the MMU translates the page number through the page tables and checks the permission bits, so a forbidden access never reaches memory and becomes a page fault.
knows: Fig 3.5's per-process address space; a guard checking each pass at a door.
subtraction: Reread chBridge-mode-p7 and chBridge-mmu-p1 and p2: the MMU between CPU and RAM, translation and the permission check, in words. Lost: one store stopped by the permission check, and the order of the steps (translate, check, fault), seen. Its TLB step belongs to Fig BR.5; the two carry separate ideas, so no merge. Phase 2: the redraw, its caption (chBridge-mmu-p3, which now leads with the TLB before chBridge-mmu-p5 teaches it) and the strip's 'shortcut' item drop the TLB; the walk runs on every access and the shortcut points to Fig BR.5.

intent: Function: programs reuse the same few pages, so the TLB answers most translations and the slow walk runs rarely.
content: Most accesses are answered at once by the TLB because programs touch the same few pages again and again, so only a miss pays the four-read walk, and its translation replaces the entry used longest ago.
knows: A page-table walk (chBridge-mmu-p2); Fig 1.15's cache keeping the last read.
subtraction: Reread chBridge-mmu-p5: the four-read walk and the TLB with its hit rate, in words. Lost: locality seen keeping the walk rare, and the entry used longest ago replaced on a miss. Keep; a separate idea from Fig BR.4 (no merge).

intent: Function: at each tick the hardware timer hands the CPU to the kernel, so even an endless loop loses it.
content: Every millisecond a timer tick hands the core to the kernel's scheduler, which saves the running process's registers and loads the next one's, because the hardware timer interrupts whatever is running, so even C, stuck in an endless loop, loses the CPU like the others.
knows: A kitchen timer; Fig BR.3's interrupts.
subtraction: Reread chBridge-timer-p1 and p2: without a timer one stuck program freezes the machine; the tick and the kernel's work at it, in words. Lost: preemption seen over four milliseconds, the stuck process C losing the CPU like the others. Keep.

intent: Function: devices sit at addresses among the RAM, so an ordinary store can change the screen or set a timer.
content: One flat physical address range holds RAM, the GPU's frame buffer and each core's interrupt controller because device registers sit at fixed addresses, so the same store saves a value, changes a pixel or sets the timer by address alone.

subtraction: Reread chBridge-io-p1 and p2: MMIO and DMA named and defined. Lost: the physical address map seen, device ranges (frame buffer, local APIC) among the RAM, the same store doing different work by address. Keep.

intent: Function: the device copies data into RAM by itself, so the CPU runs other work until an interrupt says done.
content: The kernel queues a command and rings the doorbell, the drive fills the buffer itself while B runs, and an interrupt wakes A because the device can write RAM without the CPU, so the CPU keeps working during the read.

content: Five hardware features on the left become, through the kernel, the abstractions on the right because each service rests mainly on one feature (a process also needs traps and the timer), so take the MMU away and separate processes go with it, take the timer away and nothing can stop a program that never yields.

intent: Function: microkernels contain a bug's damage while monolithic kernels run faster, so both designs still ship.
content: The real thread of January 1992 is shown, Tanenbaum's post and Torvalds's reply, beside where each design runs today because the argument was settled by use, not by the thread, so microkernels hold safety-critical systems and Linux holds servers, phones and supercomputers.

A cut adds that clause to ch4-anatomy-p8.

intent: Function: a microkernel runs drivers as separate programs, so requests cross into the kernel more often but faults stay contained.
content: The same file read crosses the Ring 0 boundary twice in a monolithic kernel and eight times in a microkernel because the microkernel runs filesystem and drivers as separate programs, so it pays in speed and a driver bug kills one process instead of the machine.

subtraction: Reread ch4-anatomy-p5 and p8. p5 says each microkernel request crosses into the kernel and out, with no count. Lost: one file read crossing twice against eight times, seen.

intent: Function: a module loads into the running kernel without restarting, with full kernel power, bugs included.
content: A module joins the running kernel with insmod and leaves with rmmod because each function it calls is looked up by name in the kernel's symbol table, so new code runs in Ring 0 without a reboot, with the kernel's full power, and a bug in it can bring the machine down.
knows: A plug-in added to a running program; Fig 4.2's monolithic kernel.
subtraction: Reread ch4-anatomy-p10: insmod, rmmod, loading only needed drivers and the Ring 0 crash risk. Lost: the symbol-table lookup and the init and exit functions running, card and caption only; acceptable, because the lookup is expert detail (law 4) and init and exit add nothing the takeaway uses.

intent: Function: CFS runs the leftmost process, the least CPU time; its time grows, it moves right, the next leftmost runs.
content: The scheduler runs the leftmost node of a tree sorted by virtual runtime because the leftmost has had the least CPU, so 3.2 runs until it passes 8.6, goes back in as a new leaf, and 8.1 becomes the leftmost.
knows: Taking turns fairly; Fig BR.6's timer tick choosing the next process.
subtraction: Reread ch4-scheduling-p3 and p5. p5 tells the tree, the leftmost pick, re-insertion and priority in words. Lost: the tree seen and one turn played through (3.2 runs, re-enters after 8.6, 8.1 is next).

intent: Function: the rule for picking the next job trades average wait against how soon every job starts.
content: The same four jobs finish in different orders under four schedulers because each picks the next job by a different rule, so shortest-job-first gives the lowest average wait while round robin and MLFQ start every job almost at once. Its strip has 163 words; Phase 2 cuts it to 150.
knows: Queueing at a counter; Fig 4.4's scheduler.
subtraction: Reread ch4-scheduling-p4 (its list of algorithms) and p8. The list names each trade-off in words. Lost: one workload under four schedulers side by side, the trade seen in finish times.

intent: Function: as a server nears full use, each burst takes longer to clear, so time in the system shoots up.
content: Time in the system climbs slowly, then shoots up as utilisation nears 100% because it grows like 1/(1 − ρ) service times, so it is twice the service time at 50%, five times at 80% and twenty times at 95% (L = 1, 4, 19 in the system).
knows: A supermarket queue that grows when the till is nearly always busy.
subtraction: Reread ch4-scheduling-p8 to p10: p10 gives L = λW, W = 1/(μ − λ) and the numbers at 95% and 99%. Lost: the curve drawn, and its 50% and 80% points (twice and five times the service time), which p10 does not give.

intent: Function: a real-time job must finish inside its period, so a job still running at its deadline is a failure.
content: Jobs of a 10 ms periodic task fill their slots until the fourth runs 12 ms and is still going at its deadline because a real-time job must finish inside its period, so in a brake controller that overrun is a failure, not a stutter.
knows: A train timetable; Fig 4.5's schedulers.
subtraction: Reread ch4-scheduling-p12. It names real-time kernels and rate-monotonic and EDF scheduling; no timeline. Lost: one job overrunning its deadline against the period.

intent: Function: an address splits into four indexes and an offset, and each index picks one entry per table level.
content: A 48-bit address splits into four 9-bit indexes and a 12-bit offset, and the walk follows CR3 down four tables because each index picks one entry per level, so one load costs five memory reads unless the TLB already knows the answer. Worked example drawn: indexes 255, 488, 81 and 300 and offset 1512, each table showing the rows around the one picked (each index below 512, the offset below 4,096).
knows: Fig BR.4's MMU and its TLB.
subtraction: Reread ch4-vm-p3 to p5. p5 gives the split in words (12-bit offset, four 9-bit indexes). Lost: the split and the four-level walk seen; Fig BR.4 draws the path, not the split.
concepts_tried: B: one table drawn large and reused level by level with a counter (its still shows one level only). C: the tables as a sparse tree with the walk in bold (tiny at 375 px; the numbers come loose from the address).
chosen: A: four listing pages one under the other, each showing the row its index picks and pointing to the next, the last to the page; the address's numbers match the rows. Gate 1 clean; not yet judged.

intent: Function: the kernel maps a faulting page already in RAM, reads one from disk, or stops an illegal access.
content: Three faulting accesses take three exits of the kernel's two questions because the page is either cached, on disk or unmapped or not allowed (a write to a read-only page, say), so the first is fixed in microseconds, the second waits milliseconds and the third ends in SIGSEGV.
knows: Fig BR.4's page fault; Fig 4.8's walk.
subtraction: Reread ch4-vm-p10 to p12, one paragraph per fault kind. Lost: the three as one decision, two questions and three exits side by side with their costs. Thinner than its neighbours.

intent: Function: after fork both processes share read-only pages; a write faults, and the kernel copies only that page.
content: After fork() both page tables point at the same read-only pages until the child writes B because the write faults and the kernel copies only that page, so A and C stay shared and nothing else was ever copied.
knows: Fig 4.9's page fault; photocopying only the page you change.
subtraction: Reread ch4-vm-p15, which tells copy-on-write fork in full. Lost: shared read-only pages diverging on one write, seen.
Held from Pass 31 (safety filter; STATE.md, BLOCKED ON TIGER).

intent: Function: a directory maps names to an inode, so two names can lead to one file.
content: Two names in the directory lead to one inode, which counts two links and lists blocks scattered across the disk, because the name and the file are stored apart, so notes.txt and backup.txt are one file with two names.
knows: A library index card pointing to shelves; files and folders on a laptop.
subtraction: Reread ch4-fs-p2 to p4. p3 walks the lookup, p4 hard links and renames. Lost: name, inode and blocks as three places, two names on one inode.

intent: Function: a change counts only once its commit record is in the journal, so a crash never leaves it half-done.
content: One change commits and is replayed after the power cut while the next, cut before its commit record, is discarded because the journal is written before the change, so the filesystem wakes at version 2, never half-written.
knows: Fig 4.12's inode and blocks; writing a plan before doing it.
subtraction: Reread ch4-fs-p8 and p9. p9 tells the journal and the commit record. Lost: commit against discard after the power cut, seen.

intent: Function: a change writes new blocks up to a new root, and one switch at the root makes it live.
content: Changing block 103 writes a new 103′, a new parent and a new root, and one pointer switch makes it live because nothing is ever overwritten, so the old root still describes the old file and a snapshot is nearly free until the versions diverge.
knows: Fig 4.12's blocks; Fig 4.13's power cut.
subtraction: Reread ch4-fs-p11, which tells the copy-on-write tree, the new path up to a new root and the pointer switch. Lost: the old and new trees side by side, block 102 shared by both.

intent: Function: a pipe is a ring buffer the kernel holds between writer and reader, making the side ahead wait.
content: cat writes at one pointer and grep reads at the other round a ring because the kernel holds the buffer between them, so the ring fills when grep falls behind, empties when it catches up, and the side ahead is made to wait. The pipe is drawn as a ring of eight cells; a real Linux pipe holds 64 KB (strip). The labels' cat and grep come from the shell line in ch4-ipc-p5, after the card: Phase 2 moves that line ahead or drops the command names.
knows: A conveyor belt between two workers; Fig 1.14's kernel.
subtraction: Reread ch4-ipc-p3: ring buffer, two ends, the waiting side. Lost: the ring filling and emptying as the two sides race.

intent: Function: pipes join small programs that run at once, passing lines on as they arrive, except sort.
content: Lines stream through five small programs joined by four pipes, each reading input and writing output blind to its neighbours, because each pipe is a Fig 4.15 ring, so all five run at once and each passes lines on as they arrive, except sort, which holds its output until its input ends (wc likewise prints only at the end).
knows: Fig 4.15's pipe; a relay of people passing notes.
subtraction: Reread ch4-ipc-p5 and p6: five programs run at once. Lost: lines streaming through, and sort holding them back.

intent: Function: a signal waits until the program's next return from the kernel, then diverts it into its handler.
content: Ctrl+C marks SIGINT pending and the program runs on until its next return from the kernel because only then can the kernel divert it, so its handler runs and it resumes, while SIGKILL at the same point ends it with no handler.
knows: Fig BR.6's interrupt; a note handed to someone busy.
subtraction: Reread ch4-ipc-p2 (the Signal row) and p9: signals, SIGINT, SIGKILL and handlers in words. Lost: the signal waiting for the next return from the kernel, then diverting; p9 does not give that timing.

intent: Function: processes share a physical page, and a semaphore admits them one at a time, so no update is lost.
content: Two processes map one physical page at different addresses, and without a gate both read 5, add 1 and store 6, while a semaphore at 1 lets one in at a time because A takes the 1 and B finds 0 and sleeps, so the count reaches 7 with no copy, and A's post wakes B.
knows: Fig 4.10's shared pages; a single key to a shared room.
subtraction: Reread ch4-ipc-p11 and p12. p12 gives the lost addition (5 to 6) and the semaphore. Lost: one physical page at two addresses, and the gate admitting one process.

intent: Function: a container's system calls go to the one shared host kernel, while a virtual machine brings its own.
content: A VM stacks its own guest kernel on a hypervisor while a container's system calls go straight to the one host kernel because a container is an ordinary process fenced by namespaces and cgroups, so it starts in a fraction of a second but shares the kernel.
knows: Fig 4.2's kernel; a house against a flat in one building.
subtraction: Reread ch4-security-p6, p8 and p9: VM against container told. Lost: the two stacks side by side, guest kernel against one host kernel.

intent: Function: one kernel answers each container's questions from its own namespace, so each sees a private system.
content: The same five questions asked inside container A, inside B and on the host get three sets of answers because one kernel translates each namespace's view, so each container sees its own PID 1, hostname, network and root, while the host sees A's PID 1 as 8472.
knows: Fig 4.19's containers; nicknames that differ by family.
subtraction: Reread ch4-security-p8 (namespaces, PID 8472). Lost: five questions answered three ways by one kernel. Half of one idea with Fig 4.21: the kernel partitioning each container. Merge: the merged card is Fig 4.21 at its slot (only the caption sits between); fig-4-20 and its caption ch4-security-p12 alias to ch4-security-p11.

intent: Function: one kernel gives each container its own view of the system and its own share of CPU and memory.
content: Top: the same five questions asked inside container A, inside B and on the host get three sets of answers, one kernel translating each namespace's view (A's PID 1 is 8472 on the host). Below: a runaway job wanting 12 CPUs is held to 4 and killed when it outgrows 16 GB by cgroups, while web and db beside it run on.
knows: Namespaces deciding what a process sees (ch4-security-p8); taps on a pipe.
subtraction: Reread ch4-security-p9, one sentence on cgroups. Lost: quotas holding a runaway job while its neighbours run on. Keep, as the merged card with Fig 4.20.

intent: Function: the verifier proves a program ends and stays in bounds before it may run in the kernel.
content: Program A is proven to end and stay in bounds, compiled and run on every packet, while program B, an endless loop, is refused because the verifier checks code before it may enter the kernel, so untrusted code runs in Ring 0 only after proof.
knows: Code loaded into the running kernel (ch4-anatomy-p10).
subtraction: Reread ch4-security-p14 and p15: the verifier told, and why it refuses some safe programs. Lost: one program proven and run, one refused.

intent: Function: one C function compiles to different instructions on three processors, and behaves the same on each.
content: One C function becomes three different instruction sequences for x86, ARM and RISC-V because each compiler targets its own processor, so the same source behaves identically wherever it is compiled. Drawn: int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } as x86-64 lea eax,[rdi+rsi] (8D 04 37, 3 bytes) and ret (C3, 1 byte); ARM64 add w0,w0,w1 (0B010000) and ret (D65F03C0), 4 bytes each; RISC-V addw a0,a0,a1 (00B5053B) and ret (00008067), 4 bytes each; x86 instructions run 1 to 15 bytes, ARM64 4, RISC-V 4 or 2.
knows: Fig 3.1's three encodings of one operation.
subtraction: Reread ch5-portability-p1 to p3 and p5 (p5 cites the figure). Lost: one C function as three different machine programs; close to Fig 3.1 but it makes the portability point.

intent: Function: once UNIX was written in C, moving it to a new machine meant mostly recompiling it, not rewriting it.
content: UNIX moves from PDP-7 assembly to the PDP-11, is rewritten in C in 1973 and reaches a different machine in 1977 largely by recompiling because the kernel no longer named one processor's instructions, so portability arrived with C.
knows: Fig 5.1's one source, many targets.
subtraction: Reread ch5-portability-p1 (1973, and recompiling replacing rewriting) and ch5-bell-labs-p1 to p3. Lost (card, caption and strip only): the 1971 First Edition still in PDP-11 assembly, moved from the PDP-7 by rewriting; the 1973 kernel only mostly in C, a small machine-dependent part left in assembly; and the 1977 port to the Interdata 8/32 by recompiling. Gap: a cut adds two sentences carrying all three after ch5-bell-labs-p3, at the card's slot, where UNIX on the PDP-7 is already introduced.

intent: Function: once bytes had addresses, a char pointer stepped 1 byte and an int pointer 2, so pointers needed types.
content: On the PDP-7 one address named an 18-bit word holding two characters, on the PDP-11 each byte had an address because the hardware changed, so a char pointer had to step by 1 and an int pointer by 2, and C gave its pointers types.
knows: Fig 1.8's numbered memory cells; a byte (Fig 1.9).
subtraction: Reread ch5-bell-labs-p5 (the 1-byte and 2-byte steps) and ch5-portability-p7 (B's word-only view, and why types were added). Lost: the two memory layouts, two characters in one PDP-7 word against one address per byte on the PDP-11.

intent: Function: p + 1 moves a pointer by the size of what it points to, not always one byte.
content: Three pointers each hold the address 0x100, and one ++ moves them 1, 4 or 8 bytes because a pointer steps by the size of what it points to, so the char, int and double pointers land on different addresses after the same step.
knows: Fig 5.3's typed pointers; Fig 1.8's numbered memory.
subtraction: Reread ch5-pointers-p1 to p3: &, * and the scaled step in words. Lost: three pointers taking the same ++ and landing 1, 4 and 8 bytes on. Half of one idea with Fig 5.5: the step scaled by the element's size. Merge: the merged card is Fig 5.5 at its slot, after ch5-pointers-p5; fig-5-4 and its caption ch5-pointers-p4 alias to ch5-pointers-p3. Gap: p3 teaches 'p + 1', not '++', so the merged card's labels, caption and strip say 'p + 1' (or p3 gains a clause teaching ++ as 'add one').

intent: Function: a[i] means *(a + i), so an index steps by the element's size, just like a pointer.
content: Top: three pointers at 0x100 take the same step, p + 1, and land 1, 4 and 8 bytes on (char, int, double). Below: a[2] rewritten step by step to *(a + 2), landing on the 99 at 0x108; 2[a] reads the same 99, addition commuting.
knows: Fig 5.3's typed pointers; Fig 1.8's numbered memory.
subtraction: Reread ch5-pointers-p5, which states a[i] = *(a + i) in full. Lost: the rewrite step by step and 2[a]. Keep, as the merged card with Fig 5.4.

intent: Function: frees leave holes between used blocks, so free memory splits into pieces too small to use.
content: After five allocations and two frees the heap holds 400 free bytes in three pieces and a request for 300 fits none because frees leave holes between used blocks, so the allocator must ask the kernel for more.
knows: Fig 3.5's heap growing up; gaps in a car park too small for a van.
subtraction: Reread ch5-malloc-p1 to p3: freeing, and the allocator and its free list, in words. Lost: free bytes in pieces too small for a request, seen.
Held from Pass 31 (safety filter; STATE.md, BLOCKED ON TIGER).

intent: Function: page 0 is never mapped, so a write through NULL faults and the kernel ends the program with SIGSEGV.
content: One write through NULL travels from user code through the MMU, the kernel and a signal to the shell's message because address 0 is never mapped, so the hardware catches it and the program is ended with a report.
knows: Fig 4.9's page-fault exits; Fig 4.17's signal.
subtraction: Reread ch5-ub-p5 and p7: NULL unmapped, SIGSEGV, and the optimiser's assumption, in words. Lost: one write through NULL followed across user code, MMU, kernel and signal.

intent: Function: a Python request descends through layers written in C, so most of the real work runs in C.
content: A Python program's request descends through CPython, OpenSSL, SQLite, libc and the Linux kernel, all in C, because C holds the layers where cycles and predictability matter, so most of the work underneath a modern program runs in C.
knows: Fig 5.1's portable C; Fig 1.14's layers.
subtraction: Reread ch5-survives-p1 (cites the figure) and p2. Lost: the C layers under one Python program, seen as a descent.

intent: Function: later languages kept C's speed or look and added features or checks, so much code today looks like C.
content: The family tree branches from C in 1972 into three waves (objects on C's speed, C's syntax on a managed runtime, C's speed with more safety) because later languages grew from it or answered it, so today's braces, semicolons and for loops are C's.
knows: Fig 5.1's C; languages the reader has heard of (Java, Rust).
subtraction: Reread ch5-survives-p1 and p6: C++ named as C's best-known descendant. Lost: the three waves of languages beyond C++.

intent: Function: every part can affect every other, so interactions grow far faster than the parts.
content: The interactions among n parts grow as n(n − 1)/2 because each part can affect every other, so doubling the parts roughly quadruples what can go wrong between them.
knows: Handshakes in a room growing faster than the people.
subtraction: Reread ch6-complexity-p1 to p3: the crisis and Brooks in words, no count. Lost: n(n − 1)/2, interactions outgrowing parts.

intent: Function: drawn in time, C++ grew from Simula's classes in 1979 into a modern style after 2011.
content: C++ runs from Simula's classes to C++23, with the style turning at C++11, so its history splits into classic and modern.
knows: Fig 5.11's C family tree.
subtraction: Reread ch6-stroustrup-p2 and p3 (every date from Simula to C++98) and ch6-modern-p1 (the turn at C++11). Lost: the C++17 and C++23 notes on the timeline, the 1993 aim quote and the three-year rhythm (strip only); no prose or figure cites Fig 6.2. Gap: the three-year rhythm goes into the sentence Fig 6.9's keep adds under 'Seven standards'; the quote and the two notes go. Aliases: fig-6-2 and its caption ch6-stroustrup-p4.

intent: Function: a virtual call follows the object's hidden pointer to its class's table, costing one extra load.
content: An object without virtual functions is laid out like a C struct; with them each object gains one hidden pointer to the vtable its class shares because virtual functions are found through that table, so s->area() costs two instructions, the second an indirect call.
knows: Fig 5.5's pointers; Fig 1.9's instructions.
subtraction: Reread ch6-classes-p1 to p3. p3 tells the vtable pointer, the vtable and the two-instruction call. Lost: the hidden pointer and the shared table seen. Half of one idea with Fig 6.4: virtual dispatch. intent: Function: each object's hidden pointer leads to its class's table, so one call reaches each class's own function.
content: Top: an object without virtual functions is laid out like a C struct; with them each object gains one hidden pointer, the vptr, to the vtable its class shares, so s->area() costs two instructions, the second an indirect call. Below: the same call reaches Circle's, Square's and Triangle's area() through slot 0 of three vtables.

subtraction: Reread ch6-classes-p7 (cites the figure). Lost: one call reaching three functions through slot 0. Keep, as the merged card with Fig 6.3.

intent: Function: each resource belongs to an object whose destructor frees it, so leaving by any path frees it.
content: Resources are acquired as their lines run and released in reverse order when the scope ends, normally or by an exception from parse() that would skip hand-written cleanup, because each is held by an object whose destructor frees it, so nothing leaks either way.
knows: Fig 3.6's stack frame vanishing on return; Fig 5.6's heap.
subtraction: Reread ch6-raii-p1 to p3: the rule, C's bookkeeping, and destructors at every exit, in words. Lost: release in reverse order, the same on a return and on an exception, seen.

intent: Function: C++'s sort writes the comparison into its loop while C's calls through a pointer, so C++'s runs faster.
content: One comparison takes five steps through a function pointer in qsort and two written into the loop in std::sort because templates compile a separate copy of the sort for each type, so std::sort finishes five comparisons to qsort's two, paid in code size.
knows: Fig 6.4's indirect call; a recipe photocopied per dish.
subtraction: Reread ch6-zerocost-p2: the call against the inlined comparison, three times faster. Lost: five steps against two, traced.

intent: Function: an object is freed when its last owner goes; a weak pointer only watches, so it finds it expired.
content: Three objects live and die differently: one owner frees on leaving scope, counted owners free when the count reaches 0, an observer is left with an expired pointer, because each smart pointer encodes an ownership rule, so the lifetime is in the type.
knows: Fig 6.5's destructor at scope end.
subtraction: Reread ch6-modern-p2: the three smart pointers in words. Lost: three lifetimes side by side.

intent: Function: a move hands over three pointers, leaving the buffer in place, so cost never grows with size.
